title: Interest Rates
in30Seconds: An interest rate is the price of borrowing money and the reward for saving it, stated as a percent per year. It is set in the market for loanable funds, where saving supplies funds and borrowing demands them, and central banks nudge short-term rates to steer the economy. The nominal rate is what you are quoted; the real rate subtracts inflation. And because a dollar later is worth less than a dollar now, interest rates are also how we compare money across time.
whyItMatters: Interest rates set the cost of a mortgage, a car loan, and a credit-card balance, and the payoff on savings and bonds. They connect the present to the future: every choice to borrow, save, or invest turns on the rate. In macroeconomics the interest rate is the hinge between money, inflation, and the business cycle, which is why central-bank rate decisions dominate the financial news. Learning to separate nominal from real rates, and to discount future money to its present value, lets you judge whether a loan or a return is actually good once inflation and timing are accounted for, instead of being fooled by the headline number.
learningObjectives: Define the interest rate as the price of borrowing and the reward for saving, expressed as a percent per year
Distinguish nominal from real interest rates and apply the Fisher relationship (real approximately equals nominal minus expected inflation)
Explain how the equilibrium interest rate is set in the market for loanable funds and how a central bank influences short-term rates
Explain why different loans carry different rates in terms of default risk, term, inflation expectations, and liquidity
Apply present value to show why a dollar received later is worth less than a dollar now

collegeVersion.heading: What an interest rate is
collegeVersion.body: An interest rate is the price of using someone else's money for a period of time. To a borrower it is a cost: the extra you repay on top of the principal, the original sum borrowed. To a saver or lender it is a reward: the payment you receive for letting someone else use your funds and for waiting to spend. It is quoted as a percent of the principal per year, which lets you compare a $500 charge on a $10,000 loan (5 percent) with a $200 charge on a $2,000 loan (10 percent) on the same footing. The percent-per-year convention matters because interest compounds over time and because loans differ in size and length. Framed this way, the interest rate is simply a price like any other, and it responds to supply and demand in a market for funds.

collegeVersion.heading: Nominal versus real interest rates
collegeVersion.body: The nominal interest rate is the number you are quoted on a loan or a savings account. The real interest rate adjusts that number for inflation, because inflation erodes the purchasing power of the dollars you are repaid. The working approximation, often called the Fisher relationship after economist Irving Fisher, is that the real rate roughly equals the nominal rate minus expected inflation. If your savings account pays 4 percent while prices rise 5 percent, your real return is about negative 1 percent: you end the year with more dollars but slightly less buying power. This is why expected inflation gets built into nominal rates. It also explains a redistribution: when a loan's rate is locked in and inflation turns out higher than expected, lenders lose because they are repaid in cheaper dollars, and borrowers gain. The subtraction is an approximation; the exact relationship divides rather than subtracts, so at 6 percent nominal and 4 percent inflation the real rate is about 1.9 percent, close to the quick estimate of 2 percent.

collegeVersion.heading: Where market interest rates come from
collegeVersion.body: In the market for loanable funds, savers are the suppliers and borrowers are the demanders. Households and firms that save (make financial investments) supply funds; households, firms, and governments that want to spend more than they currently have demand funds. The equilibrium interest rate is the price at which the quantity of funds supplied equals the quantity demanded. If the rate sits above equilibrium, savers offer more than borrowers want and the surplus pushes the rate down; below equilibrium, borrowers want more than savers offer and the shortage pushes it up. On top of this market, a central bank influences short-term rates. In the United States the Federal Reserve sets a target range for the federal funds rate, and a change there is quickly reflected in other short-term borrowing costs and feeds into longer-term rates. The Fed's own tools and decisions belong to the monetary-policy topic; here the point is only that policy is one force acting on the price of funds alongside private saving and borrowing.

collegeVersion.heading: Why different loans carry different rates
collegeVersion.body: There is no single interest rate but a whole structure of them, and the differences are systematic. Default risk is central: lenders weigh the return against the chance of not being repaid, so a borrower more likely to default must offer a higher rate to compensate, a gap called the risk premium. Term, or maturity, matters because tying money up longer exposes the lender to more uncertainty, so long loans often carry different rates than short ones. Inflation expectations are folded in: if lenders expect high inflation over the life of a loan, they demand a higher nominal rate to protect their real return. Liquidity plays a role too, since an asset that is hard to sell quickly usually must pay more to attract lenders. This is why a government bond, a mortgage, and a credit card carry very different rates at the same moment: they differ in risk, length, and how easily the lender can get their money back.

collegeVersion.heading: Present value: comparing money across time
collegeVersion.body: Because interest can be earned, a dollar today is worth more than a dollar in the future: today's dollar can be lent out and grow. Present value, or present discounted value, runs that logic backward to ask what a future payment is worth now. The formula divides the future amount by (1 + interest rate) raised to the number of years. At a 10 percent rate, $110 a year from now is worth exactly $100 today, because $100 invested at 10 percent grows to $110. Two consequences follow. First, money further in the future is discounted more heavily. Second, a higher interest rate lowers present value: a two-year bond paying $240 then $3,240 is worth $3,000 when discounted at 8 percent but only about $2,846 at 11 percent, even though the promised payments never changed. Present value is the tool for comparing costs and benefits that arrive at different times, which is why it underlies bond pricing, loan decisions, and investment appraisal.

vocabulary.definition: The price of borrowing money and the reward for saving or lending it, expressed as a percent of the principal per year.
The original amount of money borrowed or saved, on which interest is calculated.
The stated, unadjusted interest rate on a loan or account, before accounting for inflation.
The interest rate adjusted for inflation; it approximately equals the nominal rate minus expected inflation and measures the change in purchasing power.
The approximation that the real interest rate equals the nominal interest rate minus expected inflation, named after economist Irving Fisher.
The market in which savers supply funds and borrowers demand them, and whose equilibrium price is the interest rate.
The short-term interest rate the U.S. Federal Reserve targets to influence broader borrowing costs; set as a range.
The extra interest a lender charges to compensate for the chance that a borrower defaults.
What a future payment is worth today, found by dividing the future amount by (1 + interest rate) raised to the number of years; also called present discounted value.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation: Money has a rental price. If you borrow money, you pay rent on it; if you lend or save money, you collect rent. That rent, measured as cents per dollar per year, is the interest rate. When lots of people want to borrow and few want to lend, the rent goes up; when savers are plentiful and borrowers scarce, it goes down. There is also a catch called inflation: if prices climb 5 cents on the dollar while your savings earn 4 cents, you actually fell a little behind. And money you get later is worth less than money now, because money now could be earning rent in the meantime.
eli10.analogy: An interest rate is the rental price of money, just like a daily rate to rent a bike. Borrowers are renters paying to use it; savers are the owners collecting the fee for lending it out and waiting.
eli10.analogyLimits: A rented bike comes back as the same bike, but inflation means the dollars a lender gets back can be worth less than the dollars they lent, so the real return can differ from the sticker rate. The bike analogy also hides risk: unlike a bike-rental fee, part of a loan's interest is compensation for the chance the borrower never returns the money at all.

workedExample: Suppose a savings account pays a 6 percent nominal rate this year and inflation is 4 percent. The real return, by the Fisher approximation, is about 6 minus 4 equals 2 percent, so your purchasing power grows roughly 2 percent (the exact figure is 1.9 percent). Now use present value to compare money across time at that 5 percent market rate: a promised $1,000 one year from now is worth $1,000 divided by 1.05, or $952.38, today; the same $1,000 three years out is worth $1,000 divided by 1.05 cubed, or $863.84. The further off the payment and the higher the rate, the less it is worth now, which is exactly why rising interest rates push bond prices down.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating the quoted (nominal) rate as your true gain.
commonMistakes.correction: Subtract inflation to get the real rate. Earning 4 percent while prices rise 5 percent is a real loss of about 1 percent in purchasing power.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming there is one interest rate for everything.
commonMistakes.correction: Rates form a structure. Default risk, term, inflation expectations, and liquidity make a credit card, a mortgage, and a Treasury bond carry very different rates at the same time.

commonMistakes.mistake: Thinking a dollar promised in the future equals a dollar today.
commonMistakes.correction: Discount it. A future dollar is worth less now because today's dollar could earn interest in the meantime; present value quantifies the gap.

commonMistakes.mistake: Believing higher interest rates always mean savers are unambiguously better off.
commonMistakes.correction: What matters is the real rate. High nominal rates driven by high inflation can still leave a saver's purchasing power flat or falling.

commonMistakes.mistake: Confusing the central bank's policy rate with all interest rates.
commonMistakes.correction: The Fed targets a short-term rate; mortgage, corporate, and long-term rates are influenced by it but also reflect risk, term, and market expectations.

compareContrast.distinction: Nominal is the quoted number; real subtracts inflation to show the actual change in purchasing power.

compareContrast.a: The interest rate a saver earns
compareContrast.b: The interest rate a borrower pays
compareContrast.distinction: They are two sides of the same price of funds; the saver receives it as a reward, the borrower pays it as a cost, and lender-side risk and costs put a wedge between them.
Future value grows money forward with interest; present value discounts future money back to what it is worth today.

keyTakeaway: The interest rate is the price of money over time, set where saving meets borrowing and nudged by the central bank. Always read it in real terms (nominal minus inflation) and remember that a dollar later is worth less than a dollar now.

questionBank.prompt: In the market for loanable funds, which groups are on the supply side and the demand side, and what does the equilibrium interest rate do?
options: Savers supply funds and borrowers demand them; the equilibrium rate is where the quantity of funds supplied equals the quantity demanded
Borrowers supply funds and savers demand them; the equilibrium rate is set only by the central bank
Banks supply funds and only governments demand them; the equilibrium rate is fixed by law
Savers both supply and demand funds; the equilibrium rate is whatever maximizes total borrowing
questionBank.explanation: Savers (those making financial investments) supply funds and borrowers demand them, and the interest rate settles where quantity supplied equals quantity demanded. B reverses the two sides and overstates the central bank, which influences but does not solely set market rates. C is wrong on who lends and on rates being fixed by law. D misdescribes both the participants and what equilibrium does.
questionBank.skill: Identifying the participants and equilibrium in the loanable funds market

questionBank.prompt: A one-year savings account pays a nominal interest rate of 3 percent, and inflation over the year turns out to be 5 percent. Using the Fisher approximation, what is the approximate real interest rate?
options: About +8 percent, because you add inflation to the nominal rate
About +5 percent, because inflation is the real rate
About -2 percent, because the real rate is the nominal rate minus inflation
Exactly 0 percent, because nominal rates always cancel inflation
questionBank.explanation: The real rate is approximately the nominal rate minus inflation: 3 minus 5 equals about -2 percent, so purchasing power falls. A wrongly adds inflation. B confuses inflation with the real rate. D is false because nominal rates do not automatically offset inflation, especially when inflation is unexpected.
questionBank.skill: Applying the Fisher relationship to compute a real interest rate

questionBank.prompt: Two borrowers take one-year loans on the same day, but one pays a noticeably higher interest rate than the other. Which factor best explains a higher rate for that borrower?
options: The higher-rate borrower is repaying a larger principal, which by itself raises the percentage rate
The higher-rate borrower is seen as more likely to default, so the lender adds a risk premium
Interest rates are assigned randomly and do not depend on borrower characteristics
The higher-rate borrower is lending rather than borrowing, so the rate is irrelevant
questionBank.explanation: Lenders weigh return against the risk of not being repaid, so a borrower with higher default risk must pay a risk premium. A is wrong because the rate is a percentage of principal, so size alone does not change the rate. C ignores that rates track risk, term, inflation expectations, and liquidity. D misidentifies the borrower's role.
questionBank.skill: Explaining rate differences across borrowers via risk

questionBank.prompt: At an interest rate of 10 percent, what is the present value of $110 to be received one year from now, and why?
options: $121, because you add another 10 percent for the year of waiting
$110, because a future dollar and a present dollar are always worth the same
$100 plus inflation, because present value only adjusts for rising prices
$100, because $100 today invested at 10 percent grows to $110 in a year
questionBank.explanation: Present value divides the future amount by (1 + rate): 110 / 1.10 = $100, since $100 now would grow to $110 at 10 percent. A compounds forward instead of discounting back. B ignores the time value of money. C confuses discounting with an inflation adjustment; present value uses the interest rate, not a separate inflation add-on.
questionBank.skill: Computing present value and interpreting discounting

questionBank.prompt: A bond promises fixed future payments. If market interest rates rise while those promised payments stay the same, what happens to the bond's present value, and why?
options: It rises, because higher rates make every future payment worth more today
It stays the same, because the promised payments did not change
It falls, because a higher interest rate discounts each fixed future payment more heavily
It falls only if inflation is zero, because otherwise the payments adjust automatically
questionBank.explanation: Present value divides future payments by (1 + rate) raised to the term, so a higher rate shrinks the present value of each fixed payment; OpenStax's example drops a bond from $3,000 at 8 percent to about $2,846 at 11 percent. A has the direction backward. B ignores that the discount rate, not just the payments, drives present value. D is wrong because fixed-payment bonds do not auto-adjust for inflation.
questionBank.skill: Relating interest-rate changes to present value and bond prices
